1. Why mobile was hard, and what changed

There are billions of websites in the world. Before tools like ours existed, there were around 9M mobile apps on the App Store and Google Play. That gap is not because people did not want to build apps. It is because Apple and Google made it genuinely difficult.

Think about what it used to take. You needed a Mac. You needed Xcode. You needed to understand provisioning profiles, certificates, App Store Connect, and a review process that could hold your app launch hostage for weeks. If you could not do all of that yourself, you hired someone, and a decent app quote started around $40,000. That is why mobile stayed a professional's game long after the web became something anyone could publish to.

Then AI got good enough to write software, and two things happened at once. Anyone could create software, and the software you could create got genuinely better than what came before. Cal AI lets you point a camera at a plate of food and get the calories. Wrestle AI lets you upload a match and get told what you did wrong. Those experiences did not exist five years ago, not because nobody thought of them, but because the underlying capability was not there. That is the actual opportunity. Not "AI makes app development cheaper." AI makes a category of consumer products possible that could not exist before.

I want to be precise about the other half of this, though, because a lot of people get it wrong. AI removed the barrier to entry. It did not remove the work. What it did is change who gets to do the work. It used to be that the person who could build was rarely the person who could sell. Now the person with the taste, the relationships, and the audience can also ship the product. That is a bigger shift than the cost savings.

2. Case studies: 3 stories who already did this

I could give you theory. It is more useful to tell you 3 stories, because the pattern only becomes obvious when you see it repeat.

Zach Yadegari, Cal AI. The most famous version of this story. Zach and his co-founder Henry Langmack built an AI calorie tracker while they were in high school. You photograph your food, and it estimates the calories. The app passed 15 million downloads and around $30 million in annual revenue in under two years. MyFitnessPal acquired it. Zach was a real prodigy who learned to code at seven, so it would be easy to dismiss this as not applicable to you. Two things make it applicable anyway. First, he solved his own problem: he was a fitness guy who did not want to log food manually. Second, and I think this matters more, he has described his approach as continuing to release new apps until one clearly stood out, then going all in on that one. He was not searching for the perfect idea. He was running the loop enough times to find one.

George, Wrestle AI. George is nineteen, was working a register at TJ Maxx a couple of years ago, and does not know how to write a single line of code. He wrestled through middle school and high school until COVID ended it. He saw an ad for Rork while scrolling in physics class, did not believe it, clicked anyway, and built an app that analyzes fight footage. That first app made about two thousand dollars in its first month off him posting about it himself and paying a meme page fifty bucks. Then he built Wrestle AI: upload your match, get told exactly what you did right and wrong. It did over $160,000 in its first six months and crossed a hundred thousand downloads. He has now made over $300,000 building consumer apps, and he started with about $1,100 in his bank account. He built all of it on a $20/mo subscription, then upgraded as the revenue came in.

He is the person I have talked to most about this, and most of the distribution chapters below are his methods, because he is better at that specific thing than I am.

Braylin and Christian, 3AK. These two had run the entire gauntlet before apps. Shopify stores. Drop shipping. Day trading. They were cutting their friends' hair for money. Every time, they taught themselves a skill and charged for it, and every time it topped out because nothing was scalable. What they did have was an audience they built the honest way, posting day-in-the-life running content and documenting how much faster they got over a year. So they asked the correct question: can we teach this to people without doing it manually every time? They built a running app with training programs, a nutrition tracker, and a community. They are doing around $20K a month, built entirely in Rork, and neither of them writes code.

3. The pattern underneath all of them

Three different people, three different niches, three different countries' worth of circumstances. Here is what does not vary.

They built something they personally wanted. Every single one. Zach wanted to stop logging food. George wanted the app he wished he had when he was competing. Braylin and Christian wanted to teach the thing they had already taught themselves. This is not a coincidence, and it is not sentimentality. When you are your own customer, you know what to build, what to cut, and how to talk about it, and you get feedback in seconds instead of weeks.

They solved it in a way that was actually different. More on this below, because it is the part people skip.

They launched before it was finished. Every one of them would tell you their launch version was worse than what they have now. Perfectionism is the most common way this ends, and it does not look like failure while it is happening. It looks like working hard.

They charged money immediately. Not eventually. Immediately.

They worked hard on distribution and did not stop when it was slow. The people who fail rarely fail at building. They fail at the twenty conversations after building.

And one more, which is the uncomfortable one. You cannot market a bad app without a huge marketing budget or dark pattern tactics. Actually, you can, for about three weeks. Then churn catches up, revenue collapses, and you are running faster to stay in the same place. Every cash grab app has this problem. It is why "just get distribution and figure out the product later" is advice that sounds sophisticated and is wrong.

4. Start with a problem, not a product

It is very easy to fall in love with a product idea. It is much harder, and much more useful, to fall in love with a problem.

Paul Graham's version of this is that the way to get startup ideas is not to sit down and try to think of startup ideas, but to look for problems, ideally ones you have yourself. That advice was written for software startups generally, and it survives the translation to consumer apps almost perfectly, because every case study in section 2 is an instance of it. Zach did not want to log food. George wanted the app he wished he had when he was competing.

The most reliable source of a problem is your own week. Observe what you actually do, not what you tell yourself you do. Where do you lose time? What do you avoid? What do you open your phone to do and then feel bad about? What app do you wish existed at the exact moment you wish it existed?

Be rigorous with yourself here, because self-deception is cheap. It is very easy to convince yourself you would use something, build it in an afternoon, and then never open it again. If you would not use it every week, do not assume strangers will.

The second-best source is other people asking you for help. If you are an expert in something, even informally, people already come to you with questions. Braylin and Christian had runners in their DMs asking for training advice. George had wrestlers asking him about wrestling. That inbound is a free, pre-validated list of problems, and it comes with a distribution channel attached, because the people asking are the people who will download.

A good problem has three properties:
- It is felt often. Daily or weekly beats monthly. Forgetting a password once a month is weak pain. Procrastinating every single evening is severe pain. Frequency drives searching, paying, and habit.
- It is emotionally irritating, not mildly inconvenient. There has to be some heat in it.
- A specific group has it, even if that group looks small from the outside.

On that last point: go narrow first. Facebook was one university. Amazon was books. When George said he was building a wrestling app, people asked how many wrestlers there could be. The answer was enough, and the narrowness was the advantage, because he knew precisely who the customer was and therefore precisely where to find them. Owning a small niche gives you loyalty, word of mouth, and authority. You earn the right to expand later.

Brian Chesky, CEO of Airbnb, said that his favorite PG's advice is that it's better to have a hundred people who love you than a million who sort of like you. In consumer apps, this is not just a philosophy; it is math. A million people who sort of like you churn in month two, and you paid for every one of them. A hundred wrestlers who love you leave reviews, tell their teammates, and stay subscribed through the off-season. Optimize for the intensity of the feeling, not the size of the audience, and you will find the size follows.

Also, follow behavior over stated preference. People say they want to read more. What they do is scroll until 2 am. Build for what people do, not what they say. Including the things they do while knowing they should not.

One translation to be careful with. The lean startup canon tells you to get out of the building and interview your users, and that advice is much stronger for B2B than it is here. If you are selling software to dentists, ten conversations with dentists will genuinely reshape your product. If you are building a consumer app, people are unreliable narrators of their own behavior, and a friendly interview will get you a friendly answer. The consumer equivalent of getting out of the building is not an interview. It is posting a demo and watching whether strangers stop scrolling, and it is putting a paywall in front of people and watching whether they pay. Read the comment sections of creators in your niche and the one-star reviews of your competitors. That is where people tell you the truth, because nobody is being polite to you there.

5. The tarpit idea trap

I see the same twenty ideas in the Rork user database every week. AI habit tracker. AI journal. AI meal planner. AI flashcards. I do not think the people proposing them are unoriginal. I think they are pattern matching to things they have seen work, which is a reasonable instinct that happens to fail here.

These are tarpit ideas. The name is the whole explanation: from a distance, a tarpit looks like solid ground, and it is only once you have walked out into it that you find out how hard it is to get back out. Tarpit ideas are appealing for exactly the reasons that make them fatal. They are easy to explain, obviously useful, and there is visible proof that someone made money doing it. So a lot of people wade in, and most of them spend six months struggling in a place where struggling does not help.

Here is the problem with building a straight clone. If your product is identical to five existing products, your only differentiator is marketing. And if you are reading a guide about how to make your first internet money, marketing is probably not yet the thing you are world-class at. You have chosen to compete on the one axis where you are weakest, against companies that sometimes have millions of dollars in ad budget. There are studios out there with more money than you will have for years, and if the product is the same, they win by default.

So the clone is not wrong only because copying is immoral. It is wrong because it forces you into the most expensive possible fight.

Peter Thiel wrote that competition is for losers, and he means it structurally rather than as an insult: profits accrue to businesses that are the only ones doing what they do. You are not going to build a monopoly with your first app, and you should not try. But the useful residue of the idea at your scale is that the more your app resembles something that already exists, the more of your margin goes to buying attention rather than earning it.

There is a tension here with another piece of standard advice, which is YC's quote about ignoring your competitors because startups die of suicide rather than murder. That is right about fear and wrong as a research strategy for consumer apps. You should absolutely ignore competitors in the sense of not being intimidated by them and not letting their roadmap set yours. You should absolutely not ignore them in the sense of never looking. Their paywalls, their onboarding flows, and their ads in the Meta Ads Library are the cheapest market research available to you, and I will tell you to go study all three later in this article. Ignore them emotionally. Read them forensically.

The exception is an improved version of an existing app with a genuine spin. If you have a specific, defensible insight about what your version of a habit tracker should be, and that view produces something visibly different on screen, that is not a clone anymore. But you have to actually have the insight. "Mine will be better designed" is not a view.

6. Solve a solved problem in a different way

The good news is that software is infinite. There is essentially always another way to solve any given problem, which means uniqueness is always available to you if you are willing to think.

3AK is one of our recent case studies. Running apps are one of the most crowded categories that exist. Strava owns it. There are a hundred clones. By the logic of "pick an underserved market," it was a terrible choice.

What made it work is a feature that analyzes your stride: it looks at how you actually run and tells you how to improve your form. Same problem everybody else is solving, which is get faster. A completely different mechanism for solving it. That single feature is why the app was not dismissed as another Strava clone, and, not coincidentally, it is also the thing you can show in a video.

That is the connection people miss. Uniqueness is not a branding exercise. Uniqueness is what makes distribution cheap. When the product does something people have not seen, the marketing is just pointing a camera at it. When the product is familiar, you have to manufacture interest, and manufacturing interest costs money forever.

Which brings me to the argument I have with people on X constantly. They say distribution beats product. I say that is only true when the product is average, and it is a trap, because all distribution does is distribute your idea. If the idea is weak, distribution helps it fail faster in front of more people.

George ran the cleanest experiment on this I have seen, by accident. He launched two apps in the same month. One was Wrestle AI, which he cared about. The other was an unoriginal AI dating assistant, built because a creator with two million followers was ready to promote it. First month: Wrestle AI did around a million views and made $17,000. The dating app did 1.8 million views and made $35. Not thirty-five hundred. Thirty-five dollars, from five weekly subscriptions.

Same founder, same effort, more reach on the loser. The only variable was whether the idea was worth anything.

7. Reverse engineer the viral video

Now the technique that changes how you generate ideas in the first place.

Most people build a product and then panic about how to market it. Flip the order. Go find what is already going viral for your target audience, and then build the product that belongs inside that video.

Blake Anderson is the clearest case. A huge volume of text-message-screenshot content was going viral, so he built RizzGPT, which analyzes your text conversations. He did not invent a product and then hunt for a format. He watched the format win and built the product that slotted into it.

Here is the exercise, and it takes fifteen minutes. Open TikTok or Instagram and scroll, but not passively. For every video, answer three questions:

1. Who watches this? Be specific to the point of discomfort. Not "young guys who lift." Their age, what they do at 7 am, what they are anxious about, what they would search at midnight. If you cannot describe them that precisely, you do not know them well enough to build for them or to find them later.
2. What problem does this person have?
3. How could this creator show a solution to that problem, in the first thirty seconds, without it feeling like an ad?

The third question is the whole game. You are not just looking for a problem. You are looking for a problem where you can already picture the promotion. When George found wrestling day-in-the-life creators, he knew immediately, because an app appearing inside a wrestler's daily routine reads as real life rather than advertising.

There is a bonus that people underrate. If you scroll this way for a few days, from an account that behaves like your ideal customer, you have simultaneously found your idea and built your entire outreach list. The algorithm has done your lead generation. More on that in the influencer chapter.

8. The gotcha moment

If you take one concept from this article, take this one.

The gotcha moment is the one feature that stops the scroll and sends someone to the App Store. It has to be so simple that a person watching for five seconds understands the entire thesis of your app without a word of explanation.

- Cal AI: photograph your food, get the calories.
- Wrestle AI: upload your match, get told what you did wrong.
- 3AK: it watches you run and fixes your form.
- UMax: the face rater.

Every one is a sentence. Every one gives you personalized feedback you can only get by using the product. That personalization is not decoration; it is the reason the video works, because the viewer understands that the answer on screen is about that person specifically, which implies there is an answer waiting about them.

The best products in general pass this test. Press a button, a car comes. Press a button, food arrives. Swipe, find a date. If you cannot compress your app into one sentence, that is not a copywriting problem. That is your idea telling you something.

Two practical consequences.

Spend most of your build time here. George puts it at half his build time minimum and closer to ninety percent of his attention. An influencer will show your app for ten to fifteen seconds at most. Everything else in your product exists to retain the people that fifteen seconds brings you.

Your interface has to do as much marketing as the creator does. In those seconds, nobody is reading a caption. They are looking at your screens, on a phone, inside another phone. If the layout is cluttered, or the payoff takes three taps, the video fails regardless of how good the creator is. Design the gotcha screen like a billboard, because functionally that is what it is.

One more thing on sequencing, which George learned the expensive way. Push the gotcha moment and nothing else, for a long time. With a recurring creator, expect roughly five to ten posts of the same feature before conversions start dipping. That dip is the signal that their audience has seen it and everyone who wanted it already downloaded. Only then introduce feature two, then three. Each one buys another, usually smaller, bump, and it builds a story: it does this, and this, and this, fine, I will download it. The headline stays the headline.

That decay is not bad luck, and it is not the creator's fault. Andrew Chen named it the law of shitty clickthroughs: every marketing channel degrades over time as audiences habituate to it, and the returns on any specific tactic trend toward zero. Banner ads used to convert absurdly well. So did cold email, and so did the first wave of app influencer deals.

The consumer-app version of this law operates on two clocks at once, and you should track both. The fast clock is one creator's audience saturating over five to ten posts. The slow clock is the entire tactic saturating across the market, which is why the deals George closed at a $2 CPM two years ago are harder to close at that price now, and why the current wave of app founders discovering influencer marketing will gradually bid it up.

The practical conclusion is not despair. It is that you should be greedy with a channel while it is cheap, and you should always be testing the next one before you need it. Founders who treat their current best channel as permanent get very surprised. Founders who assume decay is coming are the ones still standing in two years.

9. Building your app: how to avoid slop

People call AI-built apps slop. I get why, but I disagree with the cause. AI doesn't have to build slop. AI produces slop when the founder lacks care.

Nobody is one-shotting a finished product. When George says he spends about fourteen days building, what he means is that he is prompting relentlessly, screen by screen, fixing one thing and tweaking another until every page works the way he pictured and looks the way he wanted. That is the actual job.

Reid Hoffman's famous rule is that if the first version of your product does not embarrass you, you launched too late. Every founder nods at this, and almost nobody obeys it, so let me give you the consumer-app version, which is more specific and harder to wriggle out of. Your first version needs exactly two things: the gotcha moment has to work and look good, and the paywall has to charge money. Everything else can be embarrassing. Settings can be ugly. The profile screen can be three fields. There can be one onboarding path instead of a personalized tree.

The reason the rule is stated as embarrassment is that shame is the actual mechanism keeping you from shipping, not any technical blocker. And in this category, the cost of waiting is unusually high, because you are not just delaying revenue; you are delaying the only feedback that tells you whether the idea was any good. A hundred strangers hitting your paywall teaches you more in a weekend than a month of polishing alone.

The comparison I use: if you spend twenty minutes writing code and twenty minutes prompting, you get a bad result either way. Twenty minutes is not enough time to build anything. But if you spend half the time it would take to hand-code a genuinely great app, and you spend that half prompting, you get the great app, and you keep half your time. AI is not a shortcut around the work. It is a discount on the work, and you still have to do the work.

Which leads to the thing I would put on a poster if we made posters. Prompt count is a filter. Almost everyone sends the first prompt, looks at the result, and either ships it or quits. Fewer send ten. Almost nobody sends two hundred. Every additional pass puts distance between your app and every other AI-built app in the category, and quietly moves you into the small group of people who did not stop. It is the same principle as everything else in this article.

You will do great work only if you enjoy working on your app, care a lot about the problem and your users, ideally solve your own problem, which will cause you to work hard. The care is the moat, and now that anyone can start, care becomes extremely visible.

A few practical habits that make those passes faster:
- When a prompt gives you something you dislike, do not patch it. Restore to the previous version and rewrite the original prompt with what you actually wanted. Five follow-up fixes on a bad direction compound the mess. One better prompt from a clean state usually lands it.
- Describe the person, not the palette. When you cannot articulate the look you want, say who it is for. "Design this for someone who wants to become more productive and successful, make it feel sleek and futuristic" gets you closer than trying to specify colors and spacing.
- Build the look first, then the logic. Get the framework and the visual language right, then make each page do what it should. It is much harder in the other order.

A rough time budget that works: around two weeks on core functionality and branding, a few days on onboarding, then payments and backend, plus any external APIs your features need. If you are building a calorie tracker, plug in a nutrition database. There are cheap public APIs that add real capability for very little money.

10. What we built Rork to do, and what it does not do

This is the part where I am selling you something, so here is the specific claim and the specific limits.

The general-purpose AI coding tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex are excellent, and I use them myself. But they were built for developers, and mobile is not just "software but smaller." Mobile has Xcode, App Store Connect, provisioning, screenshots at specific dimensions, metadata requirements, and a review process that will reject you for reasons you did not know existed. A tool that writes good code still leaves you standing in front of all of that.

We condensed it. Rork replaces Xcode and App Store Connect. You describe what you want in plain English - it builds a native iOS app, and you can push it to App Review from inside the browser. It generates your app store screenshots, fills out your listing and metadata, and scans your app against Apple's requirements before you submit, which is the difference between shipping this week and finding out in three weeks that you violated a guideline. We had an app delayed three months once. That experience is why the feature exists.

Under the hood, our agent supports both Claude and OpenAI models.

Two tiers matter for your decision. The $20 Rork Pro plan builds in React Native, which is cross-platform, works for iOS and Android, and produces solid apps. Rork Pro also builds native apps for Android and allows you to build them in Kotlin.

Rork Max builds in native Swift, and the quality difference is substantial. Rork Max can build amazing games.

More importantly, native Swift is what unlocks the deep iOS features: Siri intents, Screen Time and app blocking, Face ID, live activities, widgets. Those are exactly the features that make good gotcha moments, because they do things viewers did not know an indie app could do.

You will also need an Apple Developer account, which is $99 a year and takes time to approve. Start that today, not the week you want to launch.

Total realistic monthly cost to run this business: a Rork subscription, around $30 for Supabase if you need a backend, AI inference that scales with your usage, and about $12 for a verified Instagram badge you will want for outreach. George started with $1,100 total. Cost is not what stops people.

11. Design

Why is design important?

Confusing or badly designed apps do not succeed, no matter how good the idea underneath is. Your users do not have time to navigate your confusing UIs. Good design shows you care about your users and creates loyalty. That test tells you whether the app is usable.

What does good design mean?

Great User Interface (UI): making your app visually appealing. Requires attention to detail, visual taste, and developing a design eye, which usually is done by looking at references at sites like Mobbin.com, recreating small interface details.

Great User Experience: your product should be designed to 1) make your users happy 2) be very intuitive to understand for an average Joe who has never seen your app. That's what great UX is for. You can measure your UX with a technique called "UX testing": show your app to a new person on the street who has never seen it, and watch how he uses your app screen by screen, without guiding him. If he gets stuck on a screen or confused by a piece of UI, that's your signal. Help them get through it and continue watching. You will learn a lot about how to fix your UX.

Great Conversion: every design serves a goal - it acts like a "funnel" that should "convert". Every app screen has a completion conversion rate; your onboarding, paywall, and design all have conversion rates, and these directly impact activation and retention. Your design should maximize your goals.

Marketable design

There is a simple test that tells you whether you have a marketable design, and it is stricter: can someone understand this from watching it, with the sound off, for five seconds? That is the actual condition your product will be judged under, because that is what a viewer gives a creator's video. A default-generated interface will usually pass the mom test but fail this one. It looks fine and says nothing.

Two questions to answer before you design a screen: who is this for, and what interface would that person want? Feed both into the builder. And keep a third question running the whole time: how would a user share this with a friend? Anything that makes sharing natural quietly lowers your cost of growth forever, because not all your traffic has to be bought.

12. Onboarding: ten to twenty screens, four jobs

Onboarding is everything before the paywall, and after the gotcha moment it is the highest-leverage thing in your app. You can build something great, and if you cannot convert the user, nobody finds out it was great.

Understand the state your user is in. They saw a ten-second clip on someone else's page; they were curious; they tapped. They are not warm, and they do not really know what your app is. Onboarding turns a curious stranger into someone who wants the thing.

It is also longer than beginners expect. Ten to twenty screens is normal for a high-converting flow. Not three.

That will feel like a contradiction if you have absorbed the usual advice about reducing friction, and it is worth resolving carefully. Nikita Bier, who built and sold two consumer social apps, points out that every single tap a user gives you is a small miracle, and he is right. The resolution is that friction is not the enemy. Pointless friction is the enemy. A tap that makes the user feel more understood, or that makes them picture the outcome they want, earns its place. A tap that makes them fill in a form for your database does not. Twenty screens of personalization convert better than three screens of shrugging, and both convert better than a sign-in wall on screen one. Which is why sign-in goes as late as you can push it.

Four jobs:

1. Educate. Three-to-five-second visuals showing each major feature. People do not pay for things they do not understand.

2. Personalize. Ask their name and use it. Then ask guiding questions that walk them toward the problem you solve. Cal AI does this well: Have you tried other weight loss apps? If yes, here is why we are different. Then tie their goal to the product visually, showing their trajectory without you against their trajectory with you.

Samuel Hulick has the best single sentence ever written about onboarding: people do not buy products, they buy better versions of themselves. That is precisely what those two trajectory lines are doing. Nobody wants a wrestling analytics app. They want to be the wrestler who wins next season. Your onboarding is not a product tour; it is a short film in which the user is the protagonist and your app is the thing that changes the ending. Every screen should be about them, which is why the survey questions matter beyond the data they collect.

3. Build investment. Draw the personalization out enough that the user feels they have put work in, but not so long that they get bored. Someone who answered fifteen questions to build their setup is far more likely to start the trial than someone who answered two, because abandoning now means wasting the effort.

4. Create the FOMO, then withhold the payoff. This is the move most people miss and the one that lifts conversion most. Run your gotcha moment right before the paywall, but do not deliver the result. In Wrestle AI, you upload your match, watch an analysis animation, and just as it completes, the paywall appears offering to unlock your rating. The user now desperately wants a specific number that only exists on the other side of a payment. That converts far better than dropping someone onto a cold paywall.

The Wrestle AI flow in order, since it is worth stealing: feature pages, then a rate-the-app screen placed cheekily before the paywall (this single screen drove most of their ratings and pushed them past 4.8 stars across a thousand-plus reviews), then a profile survey, then body metrics feeding a nutrition plan, then a training schedule commitment, then goal setting with a projected growth chart, then the gotcha moment preview, then "your profile is ready," then sign-in pushed as late as possible to reduce drop-off, then the pre-paywall page and the paywall.

The fastest way to build a good one is to download three or four high-converting apps in your category, go through their onboarding, paying close attention to the exact moment you feel compelled to buy, and adapt those elements. There is no universal formula. Test it.

13. Charge from day one

The most common plan I hear from first-time founders: make it free, get as many users as possible, add ads later. I understand the instinct, and I think it is the single most expensive mistake available to you.

As a bootstrapped founder, charging is not how you monetize users. It is your oxygen that lets you acquire users. Your revenue is your marketing budget. Every dollar a subscriber pays you is a dollar you hand to a creator to go find the next twenty subscribers. That is the whole engine. If the app is free, people will use it, and you will never escape your immediate circle, because there is nothing to reinvest and you are waiting on word of mouth to do a job it usually cannot do.

The second problem is that free hides the truth. Downloads feel wonderful and prove nothing. YC puts it as plainly as it can be put: revenue is the ultimate form of validation. Every other signal you can collect is a proxy for someone's willingness to part with money, so you may as well measure the thing itself. The moment you ask for money, you find out whether you solved a real problem, and you find out in week one instead of month six.

And do not talk yourself out of it because the app is unfinished. Most people on the App Store subscribe before they have meaningfully used a product. Willingness to pay is driven by how badly someone wants the outcome, not by how polished your settings screen is. If you are at ninety-eight percent, ship it and charge. That last two percent gets found faster by a hundred paying users than by you staring at it alone.

Structure that works and that I would just copy: a paywall at the end of onboarding, $9.99 monthly, $59.99 annually, and a three-day free trial attached only to the annual plan. Putting the trial on the annual option steers people there, and when they convert, you collect roughly $60 up front instead of $9. That cash timing is a large part of why Wrestle AI scaled as fast as it did, because early cash is what buys the next round of promotion. If you have direct competitors, copy their pricing. If you genuinely have none, use judgment and A/B test once you have volume.

There is also a version of this that is smaller and less intimidating, which I prefer for people who have not made a dollar online yet. Find twenty people who will pay you five dollars. That is it. That is the entire first goal.

Because run it forward: a thousand people paying five dollars a month is $5,000 a month, which is more than a lot of people earn at a full-time job in most of the world. You do not need a million users. The thousand-true-fans idea is not a metaphor here; it is close to literal arithmetic.

14. Set small MRR goals: $100, then $1,000, then $10,000

$10K a month is $333 a day. That framing helps, but it is still the wrong first goal.

The real risk to your app is not that the market rejects it. The risk is that you build for six months, make zero dollars, burn out, and quit. Momentum is the resource you are actually managing, and revenue is how you buy it.

So build the ladder deliberately.

Goal one: your first $100. Twenty people at five dollars. You could literally get this by telling twenty people about your app in person. That is not scalable, and it is not supposed to be. It is a test. If you cannot convince twenty humans to pay for what you built, no amount of creator spend fixes that, and you learned it for the price of a few awkward conversations.

This is Paul Graham's "do things that don't scale" applied to a phone. The essay is usually read as advice about recruiting users by hand, which it is, but the deeper point is that unscalable work is how you learn what the scalable version should say. For a consumer app, the unscalable things are specific: texting the app to everyone you know and asking what confused them, replying personally to every App Store review, sending a hundred DMs yourself before you hire anyone to send them, and getting on the phone with creators one at a time. Every one of those is a bad use of time in a spreadsheet and the best use of time you have, because each conversation tells you which sentence makes people understand your app. When you eventually hand a VA a script or hand Meta an ad creative, you are just scaling a sentence you found by hand.

Then work backwards to the cheapest scalable version. Post on TikTok and you will get a few hundred views on nearly anything, even with no followers. Call 300 the floor. Now the question stops being "how do I go viral" and becomes arithmetic: how many posts at 300 views do I need to convert twenty people? If your app is genuinely interesting, you will beat that floor regularly, because people stop for things they have not seen. That is also your validation signal. If you demonstrate your gotcha moment on camera and it cannot beat the floor, the problem is upstream in the idea, not in your posting schedule.

Goal two: $1,000 a month. This is where meme pages and your first small creator deals come in, and where you should have one channel that reliably works before you add a second.

Goal three: $10,000 a month. This is where paid ads start to make sense, because by now you have creatives that already worked and you know who your audience is.

Do not skip goals. Almost everyone who tries to start at goals three sets money on fire.

There is a goal between two and three that startup people have a name for and app people usually do not, which is ramen profitable: the point where the business covers your living expenses. In venture terms, it is a modest milestone, mostly useful because it means you can stop fundraising. For you, it is close to the whole game. If your app clears your rent, nobody can make you stop, you never have to take an investor's money or a client's schedule, and you get to keep running the loop until one of your attempts hits properly. Graham also frames the survival question as default alive or default dead, meaning whether you reach profitability on your current trajectory without new money. It is worth noticing that a bootstrapped app founder with a $20 tool subscription and a $99 developer account is default alive from the first day. That is a structural advantage over a funded competitor with a burn rate, and almost nobody in this space appreciates that they have it.

15. Distribution 1: organic and building in public

Free channels first, because they are also your validation.

Your own network. DM your friends. Post on your personal accounts. It feels small, and it is how most of these apps got their first fifty users.

Reddit and niche forums. You already know who your user is. Find where they gather, answer questions honestly, and mention your app where it is genuinely relevant. Do not spam; you will get removed, and you will deserve it.

TikTok and Reels. One to three videos a day. Study what already works in your niche, copy the format, and double down the moment something outperforms. Spray and pray at first, then narrow hard onto whatever wins.

Building in public on X. This is the channel I would push hardest and the one people skip. Post the journey: what you shipped, what the revenue did, what broke, what you learned. It gets your app in front of people, but the larger return is what it does for you. X is the one place where you can reach someone ten times more successful than you and actually get a reply. George went from zero to 6K followers largely because bigger accounts reshared his posts, and that opened doors to founders he had no other way of meeting. We repost our users' build logs constantly, and I have watched that single mechanic change people's networks.

Once someone engages with your post, a short DM works: do you have ten minutes? I would love to learn from you. Building in public means you are building a network at the same time as the product, and the network is the thing that compounds.

17. Distribution channel 2: UGC

"Talking head" UGC

A lot of people tell me they cannot do this because they are not good on camera, or their English is not confident, or they do not want their face online. None of that disqualifies you.

Separate two things people conflate. Being an influencer and making UGC are different skills. UGC is not charisma. It is a very simple job: spark curiosity in the first second, then show the app working. You do not need a personality, a following, or a face. You need a hook and a clear demo. This is also exactly why the app concept has to be interesting. Flash a calculator app on screen, and nobody downloads it regardless of views, because there is nothing to be curious about.

If you want to scale this properly, the model the big consumer apps use is to hire college students to produce content volume, running many accounts in parallel. There is real methodology to it. We put together a full TikTok UGC playbook with Social Growth Engineers covering how to build that creator program, and it is included free for Rork members.

https://rork.com/tiktok-playbook

Faceless content

If you do not want to appear at all, faceless content works. Screen recordings, static images with text, memes, build-log posts.

Meme pages

Meme and topic pages will repost your content for very little. Twenty to fifty dollars a post is normal in most niches, and a good page will do twenty to forty thousand views. You are aiming for a CPM somewhere in the fifty cents to one dollar range.

The reason they are cheap is worth understanding, because it tells you how to shop. A meme page has cultivated a real audience, sometimes over a hundred thousand people who all care about one specific thing, but there is no face attached. Nobody is risking a personal brand by posting your app, so nobody charges personal-brand prices. You are buying a targeted audience without paying for a personality.

The case study George tells is instructive and slightly against the rules. He paid a professional kickboxer $350 to film himself using the app, then paid an MMA meme page about $25 to repost it. That combination moved an app from $500 a month to $1,800 a month, and the repost alone drove somewhere around a thousand to fifteen hundred dollars. He was willing to lose money on the kickboxer because a real athlete using the product signals legitimacy.

Here is the interesting part. They framed it as a news headline to make it feel less like an ad, and viewers immediately called it out as sponsored in the comments. Everyone piled on. Then a second wave showed up defending it, telling people to relax because the app was actually cool. All that arguing fed the algorithm, and it became the most-viewed reel on that page that month, and it converted.

The general rule is that content should not feel like an ad. The exception is that every rule in marketing can be broken when engagement is the result. Do not plan on that. Just recognize it when it happens.

18. Distribution channel 3: influencers

This is the channel that took George from a few thousand dollars to a few hundred thousand, and it is the one with the most technique in it. Influencers are unbeatable when your budget is small, because they are the only channel where a few hundred dollars can return ten times that. They stop scaling past a point, which is what ads are for later.

Set up your brand page before you message anyone

Your brand Instagram does two jobs: it converts users, and it establishes credibility with creators.

As a funnel: a wrestler watches their favorite creator, sees Wrestle AI tagged in the caption, clicks through, and watches four more demo videos on that page. In two minutes, they went from mildly curious to educated and primed, then hit the link in bio. An already-warm user gets warmer.

As credibility: when a creator gets your DM, the first thing they do is open your profile. If it has two followers and no posts, they assume nobody uses your app, and either they ignore you, or you walk into the call with zero leverage and pay whatever they ask. If they see a brand that is visibly working with many creators, they assume your rates are the market rates. That assumption is the difference between a $2 CPM and ten times that.

So before outreach: a clean bio saying who you are and what you have built, a clear call to action, three good demo videos pinned, and collab posts with every creator you work with, which makes the page look active and connected. Pay for verification, around $12 a month, because it makes you stand out in a flooded inbox and signals you are not a scam.

A base of followers helps, but it is the least important signal on that list and the slowest to build, so do not wait on it. What actually moves a creator is evidence that other creators already said yes. Collab posts do that immediately, which is why you should co-post with every single person you work with, starting with the first one. Two collab posts and three sharp demos will get you further than five thousand followers and an empty grid, because a creator is not asking how popular you are. They are asking whether you are real and whether you pay.

Engineer your feed to find creators

This is the part almost nobody does deliberately, and it is the highest-leverage hour in the whole process.

Open a fresh account and behave exactly like your ideal customer. Search what they would search, watch what they would watch all the way through, and like and comment as them. George looked up how to get better at wrestling and watched every tutorial that came back, and within a day his feed was nothing but wrestling. Now prospecting is scroll, message, scroll, message. Every creator surfaced is relevant by construction, and you never open the search bar again.

One filter to apply while scrolling: before you message anyone, picture the actual video. How would this specific person show my app, in their format, without it feeling like an ad? If you cannot picture it, skip them regardless of their numbers.

And the rule that saves the most money: followers do not matter; views and engagement do.

Green flags: 25K+ average views, a floor that never dips under 15K, performance across multiple platforms, a distinctive style where you can immediately tell why the internet likes them, and a comment section with real conversation.

Red flags: wildly inconsistent views, 100K one week and 5K the next. Trend hoppers who just ride sounds. Comment sections that are entirely emojis, which usually means low-quality or purchased engagement. And lots of views with almost no comments, which tells you the audience will not spend two seconds typing, so they will not spend two minutes downloading.

If you want volume without doing it yourself, a VA works. Give them explicit criteria, follower range, average views, engagement, posting frequency, target hashtags, plus your DM scripts and an SOP. Expect roughly $5 to $15 per hundred DMs. If you have $2,000 to start, spending $800 on a VA for the first month is a reasonable allocation, and do not haggle over small amounts with the person generating your entire pipeline.

The DM structure

Creators get hundreds, sometimes thousands of messages a day, nearly all of which begin with "hey I love your content." Yours has to lead with the only thing that reliably earns a reply, which is money.

Before the script, calibrate your expectations, because this is where most people quit. Zach Yadegari's observation from building Cal AI is that founders tend to give up after a hundred DMs when success usually takes thousands. Eli sent 200 at fourteen years old. If you send fifty messages, get four replies and one bad call, you have not learned that influencer marketing does not work. You have learned nothing at all, because your sample is too small to contain information.

Three parts. Open with "Paid promo?" or "Paid promo for [their handle]?" One sentence on what the app does, enough to be understood and not enough to bore. Then a clear invitation.

> "Paid promo for Arc? Hey, I run an app that limits your screen time and unlocks usage once you complete your goals. Love your content and would love to sponsor you. Let me know if you're interested."

That middle sentence is also a test of your idea, and you should treat it as one. If you cannot describe the app in one clear sentence, either simplify the app or scrap it. Because if you cannot explain it in one second to a creator who is being offered money to care, you will not explain it in five seconds to a stranger scrolling past who does not.

Follow up, and use more than one channel

Most people send one message, hear nothing, and conclude the channel does not work. Sales does not work like that.

The single best thing that ever happened to George's business came from exactly this. He wanted to reach a creator who was big in the wrestling world, so he emailed him. Nothing. Meanwhile, he was cold-DMing smaller creators and found one who was barely mutuals with the target, just a mutual follow. He got that smaller creator on the phone and talked him into forwarding the message. The creator was hesitant but did it. The target read the DM and immediately said he had just seen an email from this guy. That second touch is what made him respond. That person is Kayen Henshaw, and he became George's co-founder.

So: use email and DMs. Ask people in the niche for introductions and pay them for it if needed, because it is cheap relative to the deal. Follow up. The first message is rarely the one that works. It is the one that makes the second message land.

And if you have no money at all, you still have something to trade. When George had nothing, he gave his first big creator equity. What he brought was not cash; it was time and the ability to actually build. He could sit there and keep prompting until the product was genuinely good, and the creator could post. That is a real trade. If you can build and they can distribute, you do not need a budget to start. You need something worth partnering on.

Get on the phone

The most important rule of profitable deals: get off DMs and onto a call as fast as possible. Influencer marketing is about ninety percent sales, and negotiating is enormously easier when someone can hear your voice. Text also just dies. Someone reads it at a bad moment, does not feel like replying, and it is gone.

When they say "tell me more," do not send numbers. Send this:

> "Absolutely, I'd love to hop on a quick call and walk you through the integration and how I see this working. Here's my number: (xxx-xxx-xxxx)."

If they ask for a price directly, deflect once: before we get into numbers, let me show you what we want demonstrated in the video. And if they try to close you over text with "I'm busy, what's your offer," do not take the bait. "No problem, hit me up when you're free." They want your money. You are the buyer.

On the call: open warm and be specific about their actual content, because it proves you are not mass-blasting and it earns you a better rate. George once spent ninety percent of a call talking with a creator about both of them being Greek, and closed at a $2 CPM because by the end the guy did not want to say no to a friend. Then explain the integration and show examples. Then talk rates, starting with "what do you feel is a reasonable rate?"

Know your two numbers

CPM is your cost per thousand views. RPM is your return per thousand views, meaning the revenue a thousand views actually produces for you. The gap between them is your business. If you do not know your RPM, you are negotiating blind, which is acceptable for your first two deals and not after that. Wrestle AI targets around a $2.50 CPM, which is comfortably profitable there.

This also affects which niche you pick. Some industries have famously expensive creators. Fashion is the classic. If attention costs a fortune in a category and you do not know your RPM, you are signing up to lose money on every video before you write a line of prompt.

The math to run: take their average views, underestimate deliberately, multiply by the number of videos. 25K average and four posts equals a conservative 100K.

A clean opening offer: a flat rate in the $2 to $3 CPM range, so around $250 for four videos. A minimum view guarantee of 100K, set low enough that they are confident clearing it. Twenty to fifty percent up front, the rest on completion, and if they fall short, they keep posting until they hit it.

Frame it as a partnership, not a CPM

How you present the offer matters more than the offer. Tell a creator you will pay $2.50 per thousand views and nine times out of ten they decline, because it sounds like commission and it sounds small. Present the identical deal as a monthly number with a guarantee: $2,500 a month for five videos with a million-view minimum. Now what they hear is an extra $2,500 every month, which for many creators is life-changing. The guarantee protects your CPM, but they experience it as confidence in them.

If they push back on price, the strongest move is to let them open the door and then offer a CPM deal as upside. Do not lead with CPM, or it reads as baiting them into commission.

> Creator: "$350 for four videos is too low. Can you come higher?"
> You: "I really have to stay in the $2 to $3 CPM range to be profitable. What I could do is pay $3 per thousand views, so if four videos do 200K total that's $600. There would just have to be a cap of $500 per video, so one viral hit doesn't wipe me out."

You have moved their frame from $350 to potentially $2,000 while locking in a nearly risk-free deal. There is a second layer: if you pay weekly on recurring posts, your effective CPM quietly falls, because views keep climbing for two months while you paid for seven days. Track views for seven days maximum and be honest about why. Set a weekly payday, and your floor revenue rises every week.

Then stop talking. Silence is your friend. You are the buyer.

The two objections you will hear

"Brand X paid me thousands for one post." Ask one question: are you still working with them? Almost always the answer is no. Big brands overpay for one-off awareness, the post underperforms because it reads as an ad, and they never come back. That answer opens the door to pitching a long-term partnership instead. Position the big brands as the adversary, which is not much of a stretch: they rent an audience once, take the awareness, and drop the creator when the numbers do not justify it. You are not handing them a fish; you are handing them a fishing rod.

"Sponsored content hurts my engagement, so no view guarantee." Answer: That is exactly why we do not want a typical ad. We want a subtle integration into content that already performs. Our best results come when it looks authentic, and people naturally comment about the app. Only add the last part, that promos often beat the creator's average video, when it is actually true for you.

Keep an objection log. Write down what you heard after every call. Within twenty calls, the same three or four objections repeat, and you can build a pitch that answers them before they are raised. Objection handling is the highest-leverage skill in this entire playbook, because it multiplies every DM you already sent.

One clause to get into the contract while you are there: the right to use their content in paid ads. Ask up front, and it is usually free. Ask six months later, when one of their videos is your best creative, and it costs you. Never run someone's face in an ad without that permission in writing.

Make creatives that do not feel like ads

The principle: the creator is the hero; your app is a tool in their hand. They are not promoting it; they are using it.

Study their last twenty posts and note what actually performs, their tone, humor, pace, and vibe. Then use their best-performing format rather than imposing a new one. If they crush day-in-the-life, put the app in a day-in-the-life. Make the app a moment inside the video, not the subject of it. Keep their voice entirely.

How one app fits into every format:
- Day in the life: it appears during morning planning or while solving a problem. This one is gold, because it subconsciously links your app to disciplined, productive people.
- Routine: it becomes a habit. "Every night I do this."
- Educational: it becomes a recommended tool. "One thing that really helps me stay on track."
- Comedy: it becomes a prop or a punchline. Do not be afraid to make fun of your own product.
- Progress or transformation: it is the quiet reason behind the improvement, not the focus.
- Storytelling: it supports their personal growth arc.
- Q&A: it is the answer to a viewer's question. "People always ask how I stay focused."

Two numbers to make this concrete. One of George's best videos cost $70 and generated close to $3,000, and his app did not even appear until the thirty-second mark. An early creator named Cory Zader was paid about $400 for six videos, and the first one converted ~$5K.

After they post

Publication is not the finish line.

Watch your analytics closely. A good deal should be profitable within one to three days depending on your trial length, so you know quickly whether that creator is a keeper.

Plant a couple of natural comments asking what app that is. When people see others curious, they get curious.

And comment from your brand account, which turns their comment section into a second funnel. A viewer reads the comments, sees your brand, clicks through to your page, watches three more videos, and downloads as an educated user. Somebody who was not ready to convert off one video gets pulled deeper instead of lost. One post becomes a chain of touchpoints you control.

19. Distribution channel 4: paid ads

Do not start with paid ads. Ads without creatives and without knowing your audience are just setting money on fire, which is why the ladder exists. Once you have real revenue and a library of content that already worked, ads are how you scale past what creators can do.

The rule of thumb from the app studios who spend the most on this is do not run ads until your organic content is already converting, and once you do, understand that the creative matters far more than your targeting settings. That second half is counterintuitive to people who arrive expecting the machine learning to do the work. Broad targeting plus a strong creative beats narrow targeting plus a weak one, because the platform is very good at finding the audience and very bad at making your video interesting. Which means your first hundred ad tests are creative tests. Nothing else.

There is also a warning worth internalizing before you fall in love with this channel. Andrew Chen describes paid marketing as a tax on your product's defensibility, and the mechanic is simple: if you have to buy every user, your growth ends the day the money stops, and your margin belongs to Meta rather than to you. Ads are an accelerant on a product that already works. They are not a substitute for one, and if your ARPU only clears your CPM by a hair, you have not built a business; you have built a machine for laundering money into an ad platform.

The honest comparison: influencers can return ten times your money at small budgets. Ads reliably return two to three times at much larger scale. Different tools for different stages.

Two ways to run them. If you already work with several creators, pull five to fifteen proven creatives, put them all into a testing campaign at around $100 a day, and after a week separate winners from losers. If you have no stable of creators, hire one cheap, high-agency creator to make ads for you rather than post on their own page. One of the newer projects I have watched grow did it entirely this way, with a single creator producing everything.

To find angles, use the Meta Ads Library. Look up a competitor or an adjacent app. Building a running app? Look up Strava. Filter by deep impressions, because the ads with the most spend behind them are the ones making money, since nobody keeps paying for an ad that does not return. For each one, ask why it works and how you would replicate it. Then hand the winner to your creator and ask for a one-to-one remake with your app.

You will be surprised how often the top-earning ad is somebody plainly saying "Go download this app". Paid ads do not need production value. They need to communicate value as simply as possible. Static image ads generated with AI are also nearly free to test.

One planning note: there is roughly a month and a half of lag between a customer charge and Apple paying you. Your ads reinvestment cycle has a 1.5-month gap, so budget for it.

20. Learn your numbers, especially retention

Once you are doing a hundred or more downloads a day, you finally have enough signal to optimize rather than guess. Three numbers matter.

Conversion. Where exactly do people drop in onboarding and at the paywall? Once you have baselines, A/B test onboarding length and pricing.

ARPU, revenue per download. Aim for at least $2 in month one. It moves with how you market. Top-of-funnel UGC that pulls millions of low-intent views produces a lower ARPU. Real creator content that clearly explains the product produces a much higher one. A big view count with a bad ARPU is not a marketing win; it is a targeting problem.

Retention. As month one closes, watch the unsubscribes. If retention is bad, it is almost always because the app is not useful enough yet.

You can use RevenueCat + PostHog or Amplitude (more advanced) to measure these numbers.

Alex Schultz, who ran growth at Facebook, puts it about as strongly as it can be put: retention is the single most important ingredient for growth. Not a growth factor - the most important thing. And Sequoia's framing spells out the mechanism, which is a chain that runs from engagement to stickiness to retention to growth, where you cannot skip a link. Fixing acquisition when the problem is retention is the most common way founders in this category waste a year, because acquisition problems are visible and fun to work on and retention problems are quiet.

Here is why it bites harder for subscription apps than for almost any other business. You are not selling a product once; you are selling the same product thirty times a year, and the customer re-decides every renewal. Bad retention does not just cap your growth; it inverts your unit economics, because you paid the full acquisition cost up front against a fraction of the revenue you modeled.

That last one deserves the most attention, and the best example I know is Wrestle AI's own data. Retention in the first month was poor. The viral feature pulled people in, and they left. So they added something boring but genuinely useful: a calorie tracker, because wrestlers are constantly managing weight. Churn was cut in half. Then they kept layering in more strictly useful, non-viral features until the retention problem was gone. That tracker eventually became a real MyFitnessPal-style tool with a nutrition database, barcode scanner, and photo-based estimation, at half the price of the competition.

That is the entire formula in one line: the viral feature acquires, the useful features retain. Pull people in with the thing nobody has seen, then hold them with the thing they need on a Tuesday. Founders who only build viral features watch revenue spike and collapse. Founders who only build useful features never get anyone to look.

21. Where the startup canon does not transfer

I read this stuff constantly, and I want to be honest about which parts of it are written for a different game than the one you are playing. Most startup advice is written by and for venture-backed founders, and four pieces of it will actively mislead you if you apply them to a consumer app.

Network effects and atomic networks. Some of the best growth writing in existence is about how each new user makes a product more valuable for every existing user, and about finding one small network dense enough to survive on its own. It is essential if you are building a marketplace or a social product. It is close to irrelevant to a wrestling analysis app. Your app is a tool, not a network. Your hundredth user does not make it better for your first. Do not contort a perfectly good utility into a social app because the growth literature made network effects sound mandatory. Utilities retain their usefulness, and that is allowed.

Growth as the definition of success. PG's definition of a startup is a company designed to grow fast, and by that definition most of what I have described here is not a startup. It is a small software business. That is not a lesser thing; it is a different thing with different physics. Venture math needs a company to become enormous or die trying, which justifies burning money for years. Your math needs $10K a month at a 70 percent margin, which justifies nothing of the sort. Take the growth tactics from that world. Do not take the risk appetite.

Fundraising. Several excellent essays exist about how to raise money from a position of strength or weakness, and you should probably ignore all of them for now. There is very little reason to sell equity in an app you can build for $20 a month and market with your own revenue. The one thing worth stealing from that literature is the observation that investors prefer founders who do not need them, which generalizes nicely: every party in your business, creators included, treats you better when you are not desperate. Being ramen profitable is what buys that posture.

Speed as a virtue in itself. "Move fast and break things" was written for a web product where a bad deploy is reversible in ten minutes. You are shipping through App Review, where a rejection can cost weeks and a broken release sits live on strangers' phones until Apple approves the fix. Move fast on everything before submission, and be genuinely careful at the submission boundary. That is one of the few places in this playbook where I would tell you to slow down.

The useful frame for all four is Jeff Bezos's "one-way and two-way door" decisions. Most of your decisions are reversible, so make them quickly and stop agonizing: pricing, onboarding order, which creator to test, what the icon looks like. A few are close to one-way, and they deserve real thought: your app name and bundle identifier, giving away equity, and anything that touches user data. Speed on the reversible ones is what buys you time to be careful about the rest.

22. It is not too late, and here is the math

Most people believe that "apps are finished". I get this question in every stream, and I understand where it comes from, because the internet makes everything feel saturated.

It is not. Two reasons.

Software does not run out. The things people want to do with their phones, computers, watches, and glasses are an infinite and growing list. There is no finite pile of app ideas being depleted. There are only problems nobody has solved well yet, and every new device and model capability creates more of them. This is not like a physical market with fixed shelf space.

Almost nobody is actually doing this. You are in a bubble. On X it looks like everyone is shipping apps. In reality, most people still believe you need to know how to code, and most people do not know AI app builders exist. Something like eighty-five percent of the world does not use AI at all yet, let alone understand that it can build software. George can still post five TikToks about an app he has not touched since July and get ten sales.

Now the statistic people quote at me as discouragement: only about five percent of apps make $10K a month. Read it the other way. That is one in twenty. If you ship twenty apps, you are statistically very likely to hit a life-changing number, and you get dramatically better at every stage of this playbook with each one. That is not a warning; it is a plan. It is also, roughly, what Zach did: keep releasing apps until one clearly had something, then go all in on that one.

The prerequisite is no longer technical ability. It is whether you will do the work, whether you will be creative, and whether you will keep going when the first version is bad. Which, honestly, was always the prerequisite. It was just hidden behind a wall of Xcode.

Three things I would leave you with on that last part, because it is the part that decides this.

Everything is broken at some point, for everyone. YC's version is that all startups are badly broken at some stage and the job is to keep going anyway. The consumer app version of this is very literal. Thirty minutes before Wrestle AI went live at midnight, with around 4,000 pre-orders queued, the API the entire app depended on went down. Users in Japan were subscribing and immediately refunding because nothing worked. George stayed up all night, fixed it around 5 am, and woke that afternoon to find the app at number 19 on the App Store with over a thousand dollars in revenue. The launch was broken. The launch was also successful. Those are not contradictory; they are just what launches are.

Self-belief is a working tool, not a personality trait. Sam Altman has written that the most successful people he knows believe in themselves nearly to the point of delusion, and you can watch this operating in the smallest details of the playbook. It is what lets a fourteen-year-old open a call by saying he is fourteen and building something big, rather than hoping nobody asks. Belief is also legible on a sales call, which is why passion converts creators. You should also want to work with missionaries rather than mercenaries. It is usually applied to hiring, but applies exactly as well to the person deciding whether to promote your app. Creators can tell the difference between someone selling snake oil and someone on a mission, and they work harder and charge less for the second one.

Sustain it. The founders who last are not the ones doing eighteen-hour days; they are the ones who hold a real intensity for years. This is a compounding game across many attempts. Only 5% of apps on the App Store reach $10K a month, which means the binding constraint is how many attempts you are still around for.

23. Start today

The condensed version of everything above:

1. Find a problem you personally have, feel often, that genuinely irritates a specific group of people.
2. Solve it in a way that is actually different, and make sure one feature explains the whole app in five seconds.
3. Reverse engineer the viral video first, then build the product that belongs inside it.
4. Build it with AI, and keep prompting long after most people would stop. Prompt count is the filter.
5. Make it so simple your mother can use it and so clear it sells with the sound off.
6. Build onboarding that educates, personalizes, creates investment, and withholds the payoff.
7. Charge from day one. Revenue is your marketing budget.
8. Ship when you have one genuinely happy user, not when it is perfect.
9. Get twenty people to pay you. Then $1,000. Then $10,000. Do not skip goals.
10. Post organically, build in public, buy cheap meme page reach, then get creators on the phone and treat them as long-term partners.
11. Layer paid ads on top only once you have proven creatives.
12. Watch retention, and fix it with boring, useful features, because retention is not one growth input among several; it is the one.
13. Assume every channel decays. Be greedy with the one that works now and be testing the next one already.
14. Get to ramen profitable, and you cannot be stopped. That, not $10K, is the milestone that changes your life.

The hardest part of this is not the building, and it is not even the marketing. It is picking up the phone and starting, then doing it again the next day when nothing happened the first time.

Time to win.
